content.title: A ‘super El Niño’ may be looming this summer. What it means for N.J.’s weather.
content.text: WeatherForecasters say an El Niño weather pattern will be developing this summer, which could impact the formation of tropical storms and hurricanes.AccuWeatherIt’s almost time to say goodbye to La Niña and say hello to El Niño — and possibly a “super El Niño.”That’s the word from weather forecasters, who routinely keep a close eye on sea surface temperatures in a large area of the Pacific Ocean near the equator.When those temperatures turn cooler than normal, like they did two years ago, we end up in a weather pattern known as La Niña.When the opposite conditions occur, with ocean water turning warmer than normal, the pattern is known as El Niño.And when the ocean temperatures get much warmer than normal — 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, above long-term average temperatures — it’s known as a “super El Niño.”Why should people along the Atlantic coast care about ocean conditions on the other side of the world? Because El Niño and La Niña patterns actually shape the jet stream and other atmospheric setups that impact the development of tropical storms, hurricanes and other weather events all around the globe.Forecasters say an El Niño weather pattern will be developing this summer, which could impact the formation of tropical storms and hurricanes.AccuWeatherNOAA, the federal agency that includes the National Weather Service, is predicting the development of an El Niño pattern this summer, which forecasters say will likely slow tropical activity in the Atlantic hurricane basin — especially late in the 2026 hurricane season.“Typically, El Niño creates stronger upper-level winds (wind shear) across the Atlantic, making it harder for tropical storms to take shape,“ AccuWeather notes. ”With El Niño forecast to develop and strengthen throughout the summer and autumn, it is likely to translate to fewer storms during the second half of the hurricane season compared to the first half."The Atlantic hurricane season begins on June 1 and continues through Nov. 30, but the highest level of tropical activity tends to occur from mid-August through early October.The current La Niña weather pattern is expected to ease this spring, and the El Niño pattern is projected to start building in the early summer.Forecasters say an El Niño weather pattern will be developing this summer, which could impact the formation of tropical storms and hurricanes.AccuWeather“I am 100% confident of an El Niño locking in by the summer,” said Steven DiMartino, a meteorologist based in Monmouth County. “At the very least, this El Niño will be of moderate strength. I think some are jumping the gun on ‘super’ El Niño.” DiMartino, who heads the NY NJ PA Weather forecasting company, said active El Niño weather patterns typically bring summers that are cooler than average, “but more humid, with a higher threat of thunderstorms and above-normal precipitation.”So New Jersey could see an active thunderstorm season this summer.DiMartino agrees El Niño will likely impact the 2026 hurricane season by boosting wind shear and reducing the number of tropical systems. However, he says New Jerseyans, especially those living along the Jersey Shore, shouldn’t let their guard down. “Remember, you only need one” hurricane or tropical storm to make landfall, he said, to cause serious impacts.AccuWeather echoes that reminder.“It only takes one storm,” AccuWeather said in its 2026 hurricane season forecast. “Quiet seasons can still produce historic disasters, as 1992 and Hurricane Andrew showed.” Current weather radar 2 meteor showers will be peaking soon.
